The reproductive biology of Trichiurus nanhaiensis reveals several distinct life-history traits that align with its position as a large, piscivorous, benthopelagic predator. Field-caught specimens exhibit a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 2% [GSI = 2%] when water temperatures average 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This low ratio is consistent with observations in other temperate hairtail species, where reproductive allocation is concentrated into a brief, highly seasonal spawning window rather than spread across an extended period. Females captured during the pre-spawning months rarely show signs of advanced vitellogenesis outside of this narrow thermal window, indicating that the environmental cue provided by cooler winter temperatures may be a necessary trigger for gametogenesis. The timing and duration of the spawning season therefore appear tightly coupled to regional oceanographic cycles.

Regarding body size and maturation, individuals of this species display a pronounced disparity between preanal length and total length, a morphological feature common to the family Trichiuridae. The preanal length at puberty has been measured at 28.2 centimeters [Lp = 28.2 centimeters], a value that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence in both sexes. This size threshold is reached after a period of sustained feeding during the juvenile phase, reflecting the energetic demands of initial ovarian and testicular development. The ultimate preanal length, recorded from the largest adults in the population, reaches 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], although total length can exceed this figure substantially due to the species' elongated, ribbon-like body form. Attaining this maximal preanal dimension requires several years of growth beyond the pubertal milestone and is associated with a shift toward larger prey items, including small pelagic fishes and cephalopods that dominate the diet of the largest adult individuals.

Mass at birth is exceedingly low, a consequence of the small pelagic egg size typical of this genus. Newly emerged prolarvae, still reliant on their endogenous yolk reserves, have a wet weight at birth of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This minute starting mass presents considerable challenges for first feeding, as the mouth gape of the prolarva is accordingly small, restricting initial prey to the smallest available zooplankton, primarily copepod nauplii and rotifers. The period immediately following yolk-sac resorption is therefore a critical bottleneck for survival. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is markedly larger, with the heaviest individuals documented at 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams]. This six-order-of-magnitude increase in mass between birth and adulthood underscores a rapid growth trajectory during the juvenile and sub-adult stages, supported by a piscivorous diet that becomes accessible as mouth gape and swimming capability increase ontogenetically.

The early life history of Trichiurus nanhaiensis is characterized by a rapid embryonic development at elevated temperatures. Eggs incubated at a mean temperature of 21.6 °C [T = 21.6 °C] hatch after approximately 3.3 days [ab = approximately 3.3 days], a short duration that reflects the warm-water affinity of this species and the correspondingly high metabolic rates of the developing embryo. This brief incubation period is ecologically significant because it reduces the window of vulnerability for the pelagic egg stage to planktivorous predators and to advection away from suitable nursery habitats. At birth, the larva is a classic yolk-sac stage, measuring only a few millimeters in length and lacking a functional mouth. The transition to exogenous feeding therefore occurs very shortly after hatching, typically within a day or two, as the yolk reserves are rapidly consumed at these warm temperatures. The age at birth thus sets a tight schedule for the subsequent larval development and settlement phases.

At the opposite end of the life span, the species exhibits a maximum longevity that is considerable for a fish of its body plan and metabolic rate. The oldest documented individuals, primarily from cooler, less productive waters where growth is slower, have been recorded living for 15 years [am = 15 years] at an average ambient temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of a relatively slow life-history strategy among large pelagic predators, where delayed senescence allows for multiple reproductive bouts over several decades. Senescence in the oldest age classes is accompanied by a gradual decline in condition factor and a reduction in fecundity, though individuals continue to spawn annually until their final year of life.
